Since you asked: Carbon Monoxide is minimally heavier than atmospheric air. So you would think it sink toward the floor! Yet it’s also associated with fuel burning appliances which create heat, so the CO generally rises due to being warmer than the surrounding air.

You’re welcome!

And CO can get trough walls, and climb inside of walls if the temperature inside the wall is higher. Even modern heating solutions can leak CO. E.g. When the safety siphon of a modern gas boiler fails, then it starts leaking CO or if it gets not enough oxygen for the combustion.

Carbon monoxide is minimally lighter than air. It is so minimal, CO mixes the same as regular air. CO is ~96% the density of air at the same temperature.

This is easy to realize when you consider air is mostly N_2 and O_2, and in carbon monoxide or CO, C is lighter than N and O.

This is an often-overlooked item which should be a necessity in any home. A few years ago I was staying at a friends house in another city for a week. I remember feeling extremely unwell, but writing it off as a migraine. Head pounding, utter lethargy and exhaustion.

I then woke up three days later in hospital with no clue as to why I was there. My friend's birthday was the month before, and she'd been given some helium filled balloons. One of them had deflated a little, and worked it's way into the chimney, blocking the fumes from the coal fire. Because there were no CO detectors in the home, we were oblivious to the rising levels of it. It was only because her neighbour had popped round to return some cookware from a put luck dinner a few days before, that the alarm was raised. She'd tried knocking on the door, to no answer, peeped through the letter box and seen my friend sprawled out on the hallway floor.

We were both extremely lucky to come out of it alive and since then I've always made sure I have a CO detector and no helium balloons in the house
